name: Priya Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a freelance Spanish to English interpreter and translator, so no two days match. Most mornings I'm booked through an agency to interpret at the city hospital, sitting between a doctor and a patient who's scared and doesn't have the words. Afternoons I'm at my kitchen table doing birth certificates and school records for families applying for visas. I love the hospital work, honestly, but chasing late invoices wears me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the agency side look like these days?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's shakier than it was. Last spring the agency, Bridgeway, started sending some document jobs out as 'checking machine output' at a lower rate, and I said no to every one. I don't use any of those AI tools, not even for emails. Callum, my partner, drives buses and thinks I'm stubborn, but I trained four years to do this properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the hype was overblown and people still need a human in the room. I'd probably post something in the interpreters' group chat like, told you so. But I'd also say the agencies will still use the hype as an excuse to squeeze rates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, even with AI going nowhere, my life doesn't get easy. Bridgeway already shaved my document rate by about a fifth this year, and my hospital bookings dropped from four days to three in the summer. I've got roughly three months of rent saved, and freelance means one quiet month eats a chunk of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the hospital bookings and push the agency for more of them, because that's the part they can't fake. I'd join the interpreters' union properly instead of just lurking, and pay the dues. And I'd start putting a little aside every month, even if it's only a tenth of what comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved for about a day, then back to the same low hum of worry I already have. Freelance is like that. You're always one cancelled booking away from a bad month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the agency would still squeeze rates. What would that look like for you in a normal month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It looks like a message on a Tuesday saying the birth certificate rate is going down 'to stay competitive'. Last time I lost about the cost of our weekly shop each month. Even a dull AI is enough for an agency to push my rates down, and I've got no boss to complain to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about that, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Callum first, at the kitchen table, because he's in a union at the bus depot and gets it. Then probably Rosa, an older interpreter I trained with, who's been doing hospital work for twenty years. She always says the rate cuts come in waves, and you hold on.

say: **Hype was overblown**, and patients still need a human interpreter in the room.
Agencies will still use **AI as an excuse** to cut freelance rates.
think: My **rates are already falling**, so a flat AI doesn't make freelance life safe.
About **three months of rent** saved doesn't go far if hospital bookings dip again.
do: **Push Bridgeway** for more hospital interpreting days, the work a machine can't easily fake.
**Join the interpreters' union** properly and start paying dues this year.
Put aside about **a tenth of income** each month to rebuild savings.
feel: **Brief relief**, quickly replaced by the normal low worry of freelance work.
S0.quote: Even a dull AI is enough for an agency to push my rates down, and I've got no boss to complain to.
fieldNote: She was **already worried** before any AI came up, from rate cuts and fewer bookings.
Her **refusal to use AI** is a matter of pride in her training, not just habit.
**Union instinct** comes from her partner's bus depot, and she sees it as her only lever.

steps.text: Ask Bridgeway for a fourth hospital interpreting day each week
Join the interpreters' union and pay monthly dues
Move a tenth of each month's income into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say out loud that this is a choice companies are making, not the weather. I'd post about patients getting a machine voice in a cancer appointment and say that's not acceptable. I'd be the one at the union meeting asking for rules on where AI interpreting is allowed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the document half of my work goes first, and quickly. Birth certificates and school records are exactly what these tools do, and families will pay a cheap app instead of me. That's about a third of my income gone within a couple of years, and the hospital side gets squeezed next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the hospital and court interpreting, and take the medical interpreting exam I've been putting off. I'd push the union to lobby the health board for a rule that a human interpreter is used for consent and diagnosis. And I'd cut our eating out and the gym, because I'd see the document money drying up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, mostly, and underneath that, scared. I hate that I'd be the one who has to change when I did everything right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use AI tools. If the agency only offered checking jobs, would you take them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably have to take some, and I'd hate every minute. Checking a machine's Spanish for a third of the old rate feels like training my own replacement. But rent's rent, so maybe for a few months while I get the exam done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa (my old trainer), because she's fifty-eight and does mostly documents now her knees are bad. She can't go running round hospital wards. If the documents dry up, Rosa (my old trainer) has nothing to fall back on, and she's the best translator I know.

say: Replacing interpreters is **a company choice**, not something that just happens to us.
Patients need **human interpreters** for consent and diagnosis, and that should be a **legal rule**.
think: The **document half** of my work, about a third of income, goes within a couple of years.
Hospital work gets **squeezed next**, so specialising only buys me some time.
do: Take the **medical interpreting exam** she has been putting off for two years.
**Push the union** to lobby the health board on consent and diagnosis interpreting.
**Cut eating out** and the gym as document income dries up.
feel: **Angry** that she has to change after doing everything right.
**Scared** underneath, because the document money is a third of what she earns.
S1.quote: Checking a machine's Spanish for a third of the old rate feels like training my own replacement.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose a third** of her income quickly, which puts her past anxious.
Her public line is **political**, but privately she would grudgingly take checking work.
She worried more about **her old trainer** than herself, a sign of how she sees the trade.

steps.text: Sit the medical interpreting exam by next summer
Bring a motion for human-only consent interpreting to the union meeting
Write to the health board asking for a human-interpreter rule
Cancel the gym and cut eating out to once a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this should be stopped or slowed, full stop, and that governments have failed everyone. I'd be at the protests, honestly. I'd tell my friends this isn't progress if half the city loses its income in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't think I have a job by 2028. Interpreting is all thinking and talking, there's no hands-on part to buy me the extra three years the robots take. And I've got no plan for what comes next, because the only thing I trained for is the thing that goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd honestly freeze for a bit, I know myself. Then I'd take every booking I could get for the first year and stop spending on anything that isn't rent and food. I'd look at whether I could train as a nurse, but that's three years, and I'd only have a few months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, like the floor's gone. I can't picture what I'd even be in 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nursing takes three years. How would you pay for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that's what scares me. Callum's bus job might carry us for a while, because the driving robots come later, but his wage alone barely covers rent. We'd be two people living on a job that also has an end date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Callum that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd just say I'm sorry, which is stupid, because it's not my fault. I'd tell Callum I don't have a plan and I need him to not ask me for one yet. Then we'd probably sit and work out how many months we've actually got.

say: This should be **slowed or stopped**, and governments have failed everyone.
Losing half the city's income in **two years** is not progress.
think: Interpreting is **all thinking work**, so I get no robot delay at all.
I have **no plan**, because the one skill I trained for is the one that goes.
do: **Take every booking** available in the first year while bookings still exist.
**Cut spending** to rent and food only, from the day it's announced.
**Look into nursing** training, though three years outlasts her savings.
feel: **Sick and lost**, unable to picture what she would be doing in 2029.
S2.quote: Interpreting is all thinking and talking, there's no hands-on part to buy me the extra three years the robots take.
fieldNote: She understood the **robot delay** immediately and that it doesn't help her at all.
**No plan, little money**, and no time: the clearest case for panicked.
Her partner's **bus job** looks like a lifeline, but she sees its end date too.

steps.text: Take every hospital and court booking offered in the first year
Cut household spending to rent and food only
Join street protests organised by the interpreters' union
Lean on Callum's bus wage to cover rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years and no excuse, so let's write the rules now. I'd say it at union meetings and online, that interpreters and every other desk job need a plan from government. I'd keep saying a human should be in the room when someone's told they're dying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd still lose the work, but I'd see it coming. I'd be thirty-two, which is young enough to start something else. The scary part is I'd have to start with no help, because I can't see the agencies paying for anyone to retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the nursing access course at night school in the first year, while still interpreting by day. That's two evenings a week, and Bridgeway would have to live with me turning some afternoons down. I'd save hard, maybe a fifth of every invoice, and I'd push the union for a retraining fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still frightened, but less frozen than with two years. There's a road I can see, even if I hate walking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why nursing, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've spent five years in hospital wards watching nurses, and they're the people I trust there. It's hands-on, so the robots come later, and someone has to hold a patient's hand. And I already know the words for half the things they do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you never use AI tools. Would that change with five years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little, to keep the invoices coming in while I train. I'd still refuse it for hospital work. I think I'd rather be a beginner nurse at thirty-two than a machine-checker forever.

say: With **five years' warning**, governments have no excuse not to plan.
A human should be **in the room** when someone gets bad news.
think: I would **still lose the work**, but at thirty-two I could start again.
I expect **no agency help**, so any retraining comes from my own savings.
do: **Start a nursing course** two evenings a week in year one.
**Save a fifth** of every invoice while still interpreting by day.
**Push the union** for a retraining fund for interpreters.
feel: **Frightened** but less frozen, because she can see **a road** forward.
S3.quote: I'd rather be a beginner nurse at thirty-two than a machine-checker forever.
fieldNote: The extra years turn **panic into a plan**, though she still expects to lose her job.
**Nursing** appeals because it is hands-on and she trusts nurses from her hospital work.
Her **AI refusal** softens slightly when money is at stake, but not for patients.

steps.text: Enrol in a nursing access course two evenings a week
Save a fifth of every interpreting invoice
Push the union to set up an interpreter retraining fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this fairly, so let's do it fairly. I'd want a retraining fund paid for by the AI companies, and I'd say so at every meeting. Publicly I'd sound almost hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is the first picture where I sleep. I'd have most of my thirties interpreting, and time to finish nursing without wrecking us. The worry is that ten years makes everyone lazy, and nobody plans until year eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep interpreting full time for the first year and keep building savings, aiming for six months. Then I'd start nursing part time around year three, once I could see how fast the documents were going. I'd also keep pushing the union, because ten years is how long a good campaign takes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but it feels like a life I could actually steer. That's new for me, in these pictures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years makes everyone lazy. Would that include you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, if I'm honest. I put off the medical exam for two years already. I'd need Callum to nag me, and I'd tell him to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Callum change any plans, like where you live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about buying a flat in a few years. With ten years' warning, I'd still want to, but only once I'd started nursing and had a wage I trusted. I wouldn't sign a mortgage on an interpreter's income in that world.

say: **Ten years** is enough time to do this fairly.
AI companies should **pay into retraining** for the workers they replace.
think: I could **finish nursing** without wrecking our household money.
The real risk is **putting it off** until year eight, and I might.
do: **Keep interpreting** full time and build savings toward **six months**.
**Start nursing part time** around year three, once document work visibly drops.
**Hold off on buying** a flat until she has a nursing wage.
feel: **Nervous but steadier**, as if she could finally steer her own life.
S4.quote: I wouldn't sign a mortgage on an interpreter's income in that world.
fieldNote: She still expects to **lose interpreting**, so anxious, but with real control.
Strong **self-awareness** about procrastination, given her delayed medical exam.
**Housing plans** shift: no mortgage until the career change is done.

steps.text: Build savings to six months of rent and bills
Start part-time nursing study around year three
Delay buying a flat with Callum until a nursing wage
Keep campaigning in the union for an AI-funded retraining fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Two years and no hands-on part to my job means I'd be starting from zero with three months of savings. What would help is a paid retraining place, like a wage while I study nursing, and a rule that hospitals keep human interpreters for the serious conversations.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the patients, not just us. I've had an old woman grip my wrist because I was the only person in the hospital room who understood her. I don't know who does that in any of these pictures.

headlineQuote: I've had an old woman grip my wrist because I was the only person in the hospital room who understood her.
portrait: A **27-year-old freelance** Spanish to English interpreter who loves hospital work and refuses AI tools.
Already **anxious** before AI, from agency rate cuts and only three months of savings.
Grows **alarmed to panicked** as change speeds up, because her job is all thinking work.
With more warning she plans to **retrain as a nurse**, a hands-on job she trusts.
Leans on the **union** and her partner Callum, a bus driver, for support.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she would start from zero with only three months saved.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid retraining place**, with a wage while she studies nursing.
A rule that hospitals keep **human interpreters** for serious conversations.
